stories.headline: OpenAI to test labeled visual ads while ChatGPT users generate images
stories.standfirst: OpenAI says ChatGPT will show clearly labeled image ads during image generation, tested with US users and a first group of advertisers later this month. It says ads do not influence answers.
body: OpenAI said on 5 October that it will begin testing a visual ad format in ChatGPT later this month, with the ads appearing while a user's image is being generated. BleepingComputer, which reported the announcement, says the test starts with users in the United States and an initial group of advertisers.

According to BleepingComputer's account of the announcement, the ads will use images to show product inspiration, product use or service experiences. OpenAI says they will be "clearly labeled" and "remain separate from the image being created", and that "ads do not influence ChatGPT's answers". Those are OpenAI's assurances; no outside party has tested them.

The company is also adding measurement for advertisers, BleepingComputer reports, working with Hightouch, Tealium and LiveRamp on conversion tracking. It says it is working with DoubleVerify and Integral Ad Science on brand safety, to keep ads away from sensitive conversations. How those filters decide what counts as sensitive is not described in the reporting.

BleepingComputer puts ChatGPT's reach at 1.2 billion weekly users, a figure it attributes to the announcement; this article could not open OpenAI's own post, which the outlet links as the primary source. Pricing, the size of the test and the date it starts were not given in the account, and no other outlet had independently confirmed the details at the time of writing.

stories.headline: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU
stories.standfirst: OpenAI says invisible watermarks reach EU ChatGPT and Codex text within weeks. The Decoder reports detection hits 95 percent on clean text and 17 percent once a quarter of words change.
body: OpenAI said on 5 October that it is expanding its approach to content provenance to include text, "in response to EU regulatory requirements", while acknowledging "significant limitations of current text watermarking technology". In a thread on X, the company said its tools already help verify whether an image or audio file was created with its products. ChatGPT and Codex output in the EU is next, over the coming weeks.

OpenAI describes the mechanism as embedding an invisible statistical signal in text as it is generated. It says a watermark helps answer one question: whether a passage was likely generated by an OpenAI model. TestingCatalog reports that the watermark will stay off by default in the API. The Decoder reports that API customers worldwide can opt in, which it contrasts with Anthropic.

OpenAI is open about how fragile the signal is. "Watermarks have limits. They're often undetectable, especially in short passages," OpenAI wrote, adding that rewriting or translating text can remove the watermark entirely. For now, only approved researchers will get access to its detector, so they can help evaluate and improve the technology, according to the company.

The Decoder, citing OpenAI's own tests, reports detection rates as high as 95 percent that fall to 17 percent when a quarter of the words are replaced. We could not open OpenAI's full post, so those figures come from The Decoder's account and have not been checked against the original. The Decoder calls the watermark textGrain.

Reaction on X was mixed. Andrew Curran noted that, unlike Anthropic and Google, OpenAI is launching its watermark only in the EU rather than globally. The newsletter writer kimmonismus said he does not like the direction, because the pattern is embedded in the wording ChatGPT chooses. Neither claim has been confirmed by OpenAI beyond its own thread.

stories.headline: Nolla Health says Utah has cleared its AI to issue first prescriptions for acne
stories.standfirst: Nolla Health says Utah regulators approved an AI that writes first acne prescriptions, with a physician checking each of the first 100. The company says it costs $4.99 a month.
body: Nolla Health said on 5 October that it has received regulatory approval in Utah for what it calls the first AI system in the United States authorised to issue initial prescriptions. The company, in a press release, said it worked with the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence and that the Utah Medical Board provided oversight. Bloomberg reported the same news under a headline saying the AI can prescribe acne drugs without doctors.

According to the company, the system can only choose from a short list of pre-approved topical acne treatments inside structured clinical protocols, and cannot write open-ended prescriptions. Chief Medical Advisor Dr. Zaid Fadul is quoted in the release as saying: "The AI can't improvise. It can only choose from a short list of physician-approved topical treatments."

Nolla describes three stages of oversight. For the first 100 patients a physician reviews and approves every AI prescription before it is delivered. For the first 500 patients the AI issues prescriptions on its own while a physician reviews them retroactively each day. After that, the company says, a physician reviews a sample of prescriptions each week.

The service runs through the Nolla Derm app and is open to Utah residents aged 18 and over, at $4.99 a month during the pilot, the company says. It also says licensed clinicians agreed with the AI's recommendations in more than 96 percent of real-world cases. That figure is Nolla's own, and the release does not say how large the sample was or who checked it.

stories.headline: Eigen Labs and Zcash group open HashSmash, a contest for AI to attack SHA-256
stories.standfirst: Anyone can now point an AI agent at SHA-256, SHA-3, BLAKE3 and Poseidon and submit attacks. Eigen Labs and Shielded Labs say people were already probing SHA-3 and BLAKE3 within 23 minutes.
body: Eigen Labs and Shielded Labs, a Zcash organisation, launched HashSmash on 5 October, which they describe as an open competition to test how far AI can advance attacks on widely used hash functions. The four targets are SHA-256, SHA-3, BLAKE3 and Poseidon, which the organisers say help secure blockchains, zero-knowledge systems, software and internet infrastructure.

Participants point an AI agent at the challenges. The release names SAT solvers, automated differential search and formal methods as tools. Each proposed attack has to show what it defeats and how much computing it needs. An AI verifier checks submissions first. Expert cryptographers then evaluate them. All results are public on Yukon, Eigen Labs' research platform.

Zooko Wilcox, Zcash co-founder, said in the release: "AI's rapid advance could threaten the cryptographic foundations of digital security." Soubhik Deb, Eigen Labs' head of research, called cryptography "the bedrock of individual freedom and privacy on the Internet."

The organisers say Yukon has produced results before, including an ECDSA benchmark that they say beats Google Quantum AI's by more than 60 percent. Those claims were not checked here. The release names no prize and no end date, and no attack on any of the four functions has been reported as successful.

stories.headline: Figure is about to launch Hark, an AI assistant with memory, TestingCatalog reports
stories.standfirst: TestingCatalog says code for Figure's Hark assistant points to Claude Opus 5.5 as its main model. Founder Brett Adcock says it launches this week, and the first 100,000 users reportedly get paid access free.
body: Figure, the robotics company, plans to release a proactive AI assistant called Hark this week, TestingCatalog reported on 5 October. The outlet says it found the details in development materials, so they are unconfirmed until Figure ships. TestingCatalog quotes founder Brett Adcock as saying: "Hark launches this week... I don't do anything without Hark anymore."

The outlet describes Hark as a personal-intelligence system rather than a chatbot, with a home screen of widgets connected to email and calendars. It reports persistent memory covering people, places, projects and voice conversations, plus a browser agent called Handoff for ordering and booking, and a markdown "soul" document that sets its personality.

On models, TestingCatalog says Claude Opus 5.5 appears to power the main assistant and task agents. It says Gemini 3.1 Flash Image handles pictures, Qwen3.6-27B and Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite run browser functions, and GPT-6 Astra is referenced for harder challenges. Figure has not confirmed any of these model choices.

The outlet reports paid tiers called Pro, Pro², Pro³ and Pro⁴, with 5x and 20x usage options, and says the first 100,000 users get paid access free. Pricing and the launch date come only from that account. Figure had not published a product page at the time of writing, and nobody outside the company has tested Hark.

stories.headline: Cohere launches North 2 agent platform with memory and token spending caps
stories.standfirst: Cohere says North 2 lets enterprise agents remember context between sessions and caps token spend per user and per agent. It runs in the cloud, on premises or fully air-gapped.
body: Cohere has launched North 2, a rebuilt version of its platform for running AI agents inside large organisations, according to VentureBeat and SiliconANGLE on 5 October. The company says agents can now keep memory between sessions instead of starting cold each time, and that the agent harness, the layer that orchestrates multistep work, has been redesigned. Neither outlet reports independent testing of the changes.

The headline addition is spending control. According to VentureBeat, North 2 adds user quotas, rate limits and organisation-wide caps, with consumption tracked by model, user and department. SiliconANGLE describes per-user and per-agent token tracking, usage tiers and advance warnings. The platform is said to support models from several providers, not only Cohere's own, which the company presents as a way to keep costs predictable.

Cohere also pitches reuse. Skills are packaged logic that agents can call, and agents built from a simple prompt can be shared across a company so other teams do not rebuild the same workflow. SiliconANGLE says North 2 can turn natural-language requests into slides, dashboards and lightweight apps, and connects to Slack, GitHub, SharePoint and OneDrive. Connectors for PitchBook, S&P Global and FactSet are described as planned.

On security, VentureBeat lists scanning for personal data, prompt-injection detection and limits on what an agent may do, plus SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 certifications. Cohere has not published pricing, saying cost depends on deployment size. Bell Canada's cybersecurity unit and LG CNS use North, and SiliconANGLE notes the launch follows Cohere's announced merger with Aleph Alpha by three weeks.

stories.headline: Munich robotics start-up RobCo reaches $1bn valuation and plans a March launch for Alfie
stories.standfirst: RobCo says an employee share sale has taken its valuation past $1 billion, double its level nine months ago. Its autonomous industrial robot Alfie is due to launch on 4 March 2027.
body: Munich-based RobCo has passed a $1 billion valuation through a funding round that mixed new capital with employee share sales, Tech Funding News reported on 5 October. The outlet says that is double the company's valuation nine months ago, when RobCo closed a $100 million Series C in January 2026. It is the first report of the figure seen in the sources checked here.

Existing backers Sequoia, Lightspeed, Greenfield, Kindred, Lingotto and Promus Ventures took part, the report says, alongside new investors Cherry Ventures and European Tech Collective. Co-founder Roman Hölzl is quoted as calling it "an important moment for RobCo" and saying the company used it to strengthen its balance sheet while letting long-standing staff realise value.

The product to watch is Alfie, which the report describes as an autonomous industrial robot built for high-mix, unstructured work. RobCo plans its commercial launch at RobCoN, its first summit, on 4 March 2027. No specifications, prices or customer names for Alfie appeared in the account, so what it can do remains the company's claim.

Tech Funding News says RobCo operates in more than a dozen US states, with manufacturing in Austin, Texas and a lab in San Francisco, and that Hölzl has moved to the US to lead the expansion. Hacker News users sent the article to its front page with 46 points when it was read. The report did not give the size of the round.
